faq.q: Is Use finish own colour the same as spec only?
faq.a: No. Finish-colour mode permits the primary material’s paint function. Use source paint (spec only) skips that function while retaining material contribution in the reviewed ordinary primary-base paths.

faq.q: Does Use source paint also turn off extra base paint?
faq.a: No. The reviewed source lock belongs to the primary base paint pass. Additional bases have separate paint strengths and colour choices; inspect them along with patterns and HSB if the livery changes.

faq.q: Does source paint lock guarantee the entire exported livery is identical?
faq.a: No. It skips the reviewed ordinary primary-base paint pass and placement. Patterns, additional bases, HSB, explicit colour operations and target/mask choices can still change the composed paint.

faq.q: What does Lock Base Color keep when I swap a material?
faq.a: It preserves the current colour setup and tint controls during a finish swap instead of auto-filling the new finish’s defaults. It does not freeze every project pixel or disable later colour effects.

faq.q: Why did my livery change despite choosing source paint?
faq.a: Check additional-base paint strengths and colour modes, paint patterns, hue/saturation/brightness and the intended source/zone/layer target. Source mode protects against the reviewed primary base paint function, not those other contributors.

faq.q: Can I use one finish for spec and a different source for colour?
faq.a: Yes. Select the primary base for material, then use solid, special or gradient as an explicit colour source. The final colour depends on its strength, masks and other operations; inspect the composed result.

faq.q: I finished the red body and white sponsors. Can Opal add its material effect without introducing its own colours?
faq.a: For the reviewed ordinary primary Opal base, choose Use source paint to skip its authored palette while retaining material contribution. This is not whole-project pixel identity: check extra bases, patterns, colour adjustments and target coverage.

faq.q: Does every Foundation finish leave my colour alone?
faq.a: The shelf alone does not guarantee that. Use source paint skips the reviewed ordinary primary base paint pass, including the five colour-generating Foundation exceptions. Finish-colour mode can add their palettes; patterns, additional bases and HSB can still alter paint.

faq.q: Can I keep sponsor artwork and use a textured Foundation spec?
faq.a: Yes for the reviewed ordinary primary-base path: choose a textured material and Use source paint (spec only). This skips its paint function; inspect the other paint contributors and the intended target separately.

faq.q: I want matte sponsors on a glossy body without repainting the logos. What should I separate?
faq.a: Separate the material targets for the body and sponsors. Inspect the actual layers: use separate restricted zones only if their artwork is genuinely separate. For shared or flat artwork use a checked local mask or separate the artwork first. Use source paint for primary material-only changes, but remember that it does not preserve sponsor shine.

faq.q: I need matte numbers on shiny paint. Which surface should I isolate?
faq.a: Isolate the actual number artwork separately from the body material target. Inspect the layer contents and visible coverage; if they share a layer or a flat image, use a checked local mask or separate the artwork. Source paint protects the reviewed primary paint pass, not the chosen material response.

faq.q: Is source paint enough to keep numbers matte on a glossy body?
faq.a: No. Source paint retains the reviewed primary artwork pass while spec remains active. Keep the number material outside the glossy body target or give it a separate checked material target.

faq.q: Can increasing roughness change the reflected appearance without repainting RGB?
faq.a: Yes. Roughness controls material response separately from decorative RGB. The apparent colour and reflections can change even when source paint pixels are retained. Check paint and spec separately and inspect other contributors before concluding the final composition preserves artwork.

articles.title: Which part of a finish does the work
articles.summary: Surface intent describes the emphasis of a finish: material response, pattern structure, image colour, fine structural colour, or both paint and material. It is metadata, not proof that an individual paint function is inactive or that source artwork stays unchanged.
articles.what: The canonical intent map classifies category emphasis, and its comments describe design/audit goals. Spec-driven means material-focused, not a verified paint_none contract for every entry. Reviewed plain Foundation identities are constant-material/paint-none examples, while reviewed gem/shift identities can carry colour. Foundation EFX is mapped Full and has mixed individual paint behavior. Ghost Hex/Stripes/Diamonds are mapped spec-driven but their active factory varies all three material channels and can add small RGB tint/shadow/edge marks. Pattern-design, pattern-image and fine-structural-colour labels likewise describe emphasis; inspect actual exact identities/functions for colour, geometry, scale and preservation facts.

You want to predict how a finish will react to your colour

Spec-driven: choose it for shine and set colour separately.

tips: Classic Foundation has no texture on purpose. Grain and flake belong in patterns and spec overlays.
The Foundation EFX shelf carries its own paint and shine, so it is a full finish, not spec-only.
pitfalls: Do not infer paint preservation, material-channel exclusivity or accepted native appearance from category intent.
Feature-scale recommendations require the actual finish and template; a category label supplies no physical calibration.

deep.heading: What the groups actually are
deep.body: Spec-driven: Foundation, Clearcoat and Ghost Geometry. Fine structural colour: Fractured Cryptid, Morpho, Bloom and Petri, Neon and ASTRA. Pattern-design: carbon, geometric, guilloche, panel quilting, optical, op-art, mathematical and fractal, decades, ornamental, artistic and cultural. Pattern-image: Cultural, with one single exception for a Celtic spiral. Everything else, including Foundation EFX, is a full finish. The grouping is a lookup by shelf name.

deep.heading: It describes the catalogue, it does not change the render
deep.body: The render path is the same for every finish. The group is used by the catalogue checks and the thumbnail baking: spec-driven finishes are judged mostly on their spec (and their thumbnail shows the spec channel), pattern-design finishes are judged on shape, and fine structural colour finishes on their micro detail. What makes a Foundation finish spec-only in practice is its data: it has no paint routine and a flat spec, so with Use source paint it cannot touch your colours.

deep.heading: How to use the group when choosing
deep.body: Spec-driven: pick for shine and set colour separately. Pattern-design: pick for the shape and recolour freely. Fine structural colour: pick for the effect, leave scale alone and judge it on the car, because scaling it up weakens the colour that shows through the shine. Full: use as it comes and adjust.

faq.q: Does the group change how a finish renders?
faq.a: The intent label is metadata used to describe category emphasis and audit/preview policy. The exact registered paint/spec functions and composition path determine actual changes; the label alone does not establish preservation, physical geometry or native appearance.

faq.q: Why is Foundation EFX a full finish?
faq.a: Foundation EFX contains different paint/spec behaviors. Some registered paint stages pass input RGB through, while others apply effect paint. The shelf name does not make every entry a full repainting finish; inspect the individual finish and final zone outputs.

faq.q: Where does Ghost Geometry sit?
faq.a: The category is mapped spec-driven, meaning material-focused. The inspected active Ghost Hex/Stripes/Diamonds factory is not clearcoat-only or paint_none: it varies metallic, roughness and clearcoat and can add small RGB marks.

faq.q: What is pattern-image?
faq.a: Patterns that carry real colour from an image, the Cultural family.

faq.q: Does a spec-driven category prove that its paint function does nothing?
faq.a: No. Intent describes emphasis. The inspected Ghost factory includes paint tint/shadow/edge marks, while the reviewed plain Foundation identities are specifically bound to paint_none. Verify the exact entry and composed output.

articles.title: Foundation and Foundation EFX
articles.summary: Foundation offers plain material responses plus five colour-bearing gem/shift exceptions. Foundation EFX has46 active effects; check the individual finish because its paint and spec behavior is not uniform.
articles.what: For a simple change of sheen or metal response without built-in texture, choose one of the20 plain Foundation material cells and Use source paint (spec only). The Foundation shelf also includes Opal, Moonstone, Spectraflame, Chameleon and Hypershift Spectral, which are not plain paint-preserving cells. Foundation EFX offers46 effect finishes, including orange peel, damascus, gold leaf, weathering and other surface stories. The current registered paint stages for Holographic Drift, Frost Fractal and Frost Mercury Duo pass their input paint through. Other EFX entries have effect paint functions: do not promise unchanged artwork merely because their category includes Foundation. Colour-source modes and the rest of the zone stack also matter. Compare the paint output separately from spec before committing to a livery-wide effect.

For an EFX surface effect, inspect the individual finish and restrict its zone to the intended artwork. A shelf label is not proof of colour preservation or sponsor safety.

deep.heading: Foundation versus Foundation EFX
deep.body: Foundation (25 finishes) is flat spec, no paint, keeps your colours. Foundation EFX (46 finishes) carries a surface story of its own: orange peel, wire-brushed metal, damascus steel, gold leaf, snow crust, chalked paint, cast iron. Only 11 percent of EFX bring their own colours, so most still take yours. EFX averages metal 107, roughness 82, coat 82 with a large spread (metal varies by about 66), and 18 of its 46 are micro-detail.

deep.heading: When EFX is the right choice
deep.body: Use EFX when you want the surface to read from afar without building it. Use Foundation plus a spec overlay when you want control over the texture and its strength. Do not stack a heavy pattern on an EFX finish; it already has texture and the two fight.

faq.q: Are Foundation EFX material numbers constant settings for the whole finish?
faq.a: No. The43 rebuilt entries generate spatial spec from a field and material deck. Registry M/R/CC values are anchors, not constant exported values or calibrated slider recommendations.

faq.q: Does EFX keep my colours?
faq.a: It depends on the individual finish and colour-source mode. Do not use the old percentage claim as a guarantee. The registered paint stages for Holographic Drift, Frost Fractal and Frost Mercury Duo pass their input through; many other EFX finishes have effect paint functions. Final paint can also be changed elsewhere in the zone stack.

faq.q: Why is EFX a full finish?
faq.a: Foundation EFX is a category of effects, not one uniform render contract. Some members preserve their input at the registered paint stage and provide spec effects; other members have effect paint functions. Judge the actual finish and final outputs, rather than assuming the whole shelf repaints or preserves artwork.

Foundation or Foundation EFX: which should I choose?
faq.a: Use a plain Foundation material for a simple sheen or metallic response without built-in texture. Choose Foundation EFX when you want a specific surface effect, then inspect its individual paint/spec behavior. For an existing livery, preserve source colour and limit the zone to artwork you intend to change.

faq.q: Are all Foundation EFX finishes spec only?
faq.a: No. Foundation EFX contains different paint stages. Three current entries use paint_passthrough, but other entries have effect paint functions. The category name alone cannot establish whether your final paint stays unchanged.

faq.q: Which EFX paint stages pass the source through?
faq.a: Holographic Drift (efx_holographic_drift), Frost Fractal (efx_frost_fractal) and Frost Mercury Duo (efx_frost_mercury_duo) currently register paint_passthrough. That function copies its input RGB at the paint stage. This does not establish that later colour controls, patterns or other zone operations preserve the finished paint.

faq.q: Does choosing Foundation EFX protect sponsor colours?
faq.a: No category guarantees that. Inspect layer and zone targeting so the effect reaches only intended body artwork. A paint-preserving stage can still change sponsor material response when the same zone covers sponsors. Check both paint and spec outputs.

faq.q: Why would I choose plain Foundation instead of an effect finish?
faq.a: A plain Foundation cell gives a predictable constant material starting point without built-in grain or flake. It is useful when you want to keep the original artwork and choose its sheen separately. Effects can add surface character, but need their own paint/spec and readability checks.

faq.q: Can I assume an EFX name guarantees its visible result?
faq.a: No. Its name helps you find a candidate, but effective colour mode, scale, zone coverage, overlays and the actual render determine the result. Treat catalog descriptions as selection clues, then verify the intended effect on your artwork.

articles.what: ASTRA uses per-finish builders adopted through a shared adapter. Metallic, roughness and clearcoat fields vary with named masks; they are not paint colours or measured physical fractions.

Use the exact named material guides for all 50 currently active identities; source inspection still does not establish native appearance.

Compare separate material channels and check coverage/source protection.
Compare the actual car at useful viewing distances before accepting scale, readability or lighting behaviour.

Try simpler neighbours as a design option; actual readability still needs inspection.

deep.heading: Construction and limits
deep.body: All 50 current active ASTRA identities have final adapters and actual builder material expressions traced in the October12 audit. The adapter constructs paint/spec together with authored seed42 and resizes outputs for requested shapes. Enrichment, clipping and engine composition affect final values. No rendering, actual car appearance, physical emission, geometry or UV calibration was tested.

Read paint and material channels separately.

faq.q: Will changing the seed give me a new ASTRA construction?
faq.a: The public ASTRA paint/spec adapters use authored construction seed 42 regardless of the job seed. The research builder remains seedable, but changing an editor job seed is not proof of a new construction.

faq.q: Are all ASTRA finishes proven to have fine 8–32 pixel features and look good on every car?
faq.a: No. The identity contract states a fine-detail intention, but this audit did not render or validate every finish at native or picker scale. Verify actual detail, car scale, material contrast and readability before accepting a recommendation.

articles.title: Ghost Geometry and Clearcoat
articles.summary: Ghost Panel preserves input RGB in its own paint function and uses fixed metallic/roughness with varying clearcoat. Ghost Hex, Stripes and Diamonds use a different factory that can alter RGB and all three spec channels. Check exact identity and the whole composition; names do not guarantee visibility or preservation.
articles.what: The current filtered picker contains 11 Ghost Geometry identities. Ten final registrations point to the fast factory reviewed for Ghost Hex, Stripes and Diamonds: it varies metallic, roughness and clearcoat and can add small RGB tint, shadow and edge marks. Ghost Panel is a distinct exception: its paint function returns a defensive copy of input RGB; its spec function holds M=200 and G=40 and varies B clearcoat through a noise-driven sigmoid between bounds 16 and 90. These are callable-level facts, not a guarantee that other contributors leave the finished paint untouched. No field or render function was executed in this review. Spec-driven is intent, not proof of paint_none or clearcoat-only behavior. Texture coordinates do not prove physical geometry or UV placement. Legacy Clearcoat IDs cc_overspray_halo, cc_panel_fade, cc_panel_pool and cc_wet_zone remain in a raw Glass & Surface list but are absent from the inspected filtered picker and final monolithic registry. Do not recommend those unavailable identities or infer Clearcoat membership from a cc prefix.

You need to compare paint preservation for exact Ghost identities.
how: Choose the exact currently reachable identity; do not select a similarly named Ghost finish from an unrelated family.
Inspect the paint image and all three material-channel images separately; check actual contributors and target coverage.
If protecting sponsors or numbers, isolate and inspect the intended source artwork and target before applying; a category label is not preservation proof.
Compare the actual car under relevant lighting and camera views. No universal angle threshold or guaranteed visibility is established.
tips: Spec variation can exist in M/G/B together; inspect each channel rather than assuming all character is in clearcoat.
pitfalls: Do not generalize Ghost Panel paint preservation to Ghost Hex or the whole family.
An unchanged single paint function does not protect artwork from other layers, patterns, bases or colour controls.
No universal hidden-at-an-angle or daylight/night suitability guarantee is established.
Raw legacy category lists are not current selectable inventory.

deep.heading: Inspected paint contribution
deep.body: Fast factory uses tint blend scaled0.060, shadow subtraction0.020 and edge addition0.025 under its mask/paint strength. These coefficients are source behavior, not a measured percentage of perceived colour change.

deep.heading: Ghost Panel exception
deep.body: The registered paint function copies input RGB rather than drawing the factory tint/shadow/edge marks. Its spec function has fixed M=200/G=40, mask-derived alpha and variable B driven by noise and sigmoid steepness 12×sm. Bounds are not a measured per-car appearance or guaranteed attained extrema. Final composition can still affect the channels.

deep.heading: Picker tint versus final paint
deep.body: The inspected active ghost_hex entry has reference tint #445566. This is not a material-channel byte tuple or proof of final RGB or rendered lighting. A finish name, exact identity, reference swatch, generated pattern and composed paint are separate facts.

faq.q: Does Ghost Hex Grid only change clearcoat while leaving RGB paint untouched?
faq.a: No. Its inspected final spec function varies metallic, roughness and clearcoat, and its paint function can add small tint, shadow and edge marks. Spec-driven is an intent label, not proof of paint_none or zero RGB changes.

faq.q: Does a spec-driven category prove that its paint function does nothing?
faq.a: No. For example, the inspected active Ghost Hex/Stripes/Diamonds factory includes paint-side tint, shadow and edge changes. Check the exact callable and composed output; do not infer source-artwork preservation from a family label.

faq.q: Will Ghost Stripes stay invisible head-on and appear at every angle?
faq.a: That is not verified. The source generates texture/material fields without a camera-angle visibility threshold. The actual rendered car and lighting determine the apparent response, and the paint function can also supply small visible RGB marks.

faq.q: Is a Ghost Geometry shape new physical geometry on my car?
faq.a: The reviewed functions generate paint and spec texture arrays. They do not create new car body geometry. Their image coordinates also do not establish which physical panels or UV islands carry the pattern.

faq.q: If I see nothing with a ghost finish, should I assume it is broken?
faq.a: First confirm exact identity, target coverage, paint/spec contribution and the composed channel images. Then inspect the actual car under relevant lighting. A flat paint image alone does not prove missing material structure, but visibility is not guaranteed by the name either.

faq.q: Are Ghost Geometry and every Clearcoat finish guaranteed to behave identically?
faq.a: No. Ghost Panel alone has a different registered paint/spec construction from the reviewed Ghost Hex factory. Four legacy Clearcoat IDs are unavailable in the inspected filtered picker. Exact identity and final composition matter; no universal native appearance is established.

faq.q: How many Ghost Geometry identities are in the current filtered picker?
faq.a: The inspected current export contains11named Ghost Geometry identities. This is reachable membership, not11verified unique constructions or native recommendations. Other finishes containing Ghost in their names are different identities.

faq.q: Does Ghost Panel change my RGB paint like Ghost Hex does?
faq.a: Their registered paint functions differ. Ghost Panel returns a copy of input RGB, while the reviewed Ghost Hex factory can add small tint, shadow and edge marks. That single-function preservation does not guarantee untouched final paint when other contributors or controls are active.

faq.q: Does Ghost Panel vary metallic and roughness across its pattern?
faq.a: Its inspected spec function holds M=200 and G=40 across the array and varies B clearcoat from a noise-driven sigmoid. This is distinct from the reviewed Ghost Hex factory, which varies all three channels. Final composition and contribution settings can still alter the delivered spec.

faq.q: Does Ghost Panel guarantee a hidden pattern at every camera angle?
faq.a: No. The source generates texture and clearcoat values without a camera-angle visibility threshold. Its docstring describes an intended reveal, but this review has not established per-car or per-lighting visibility.

faq.q: Can I choose Clearcoat Panel Pool from the current filtered picker?
faq.a: The legacy cc_panel_pool ID is absent from the inspected current filtered picker and final monolithic registry, along with cc_panel_fade, cc_overspray_halo and cc_wet_zone. A raw Glass & Surface list still mentioning them is not selectable membership. Choose a currently available identity instead.

faq.q: Does Ghost Hex Grid have a hex colour code?
faq.a: The inspected picker entry uses #445566 as its reference swatch tint. Hex in the finish name describes hexagonal pattern construction, not an instruction to enter a colour code. That picker tint is not a guarantee of final car RGB: the actual paint depends on its source, contribution settings and other composed effects.

faq.q: What is the hex code for Ghost Hex Grid?
faq.a: Its inspected current picker reference tint is #445566. This is a swatch/catalog reference, not a universal final paint colour or a material-channel setting. The finish is identified by ghost_hex; its hexagonal pattern and material response are separate from a colour code.

faq.q: Is the Ghost Hex Grid swatch #445566 a guarantee of the final car colour?
faq.a: No. #445566 is the inspected catalog reference tint. The reviewed paint function starts from its supplied RGB and can add small tint, shadow and edge marks; contribution settings and other effects also matter. Check the composed paint rather than assuming every pixel or the lit car will equal the picker swatch.

faq.q: Does Hex in Ghost Hex Grid mean a colour code or a hexagonal pattern?
faq.a: Hex in this finish name refers to hexagonal pattern construction. The exact identity is ghost_hex. The picker also has a reference swatch #445566, but that colour code is separate from pattern construction and does not guarantee final car colour.

articles.title: Choosing colour-shift looks without assuming automatic hue changes
articles.summary: Reviewed Chameleon Amethyst, Arctic and Copper generate colour-bearing paint and material textures. Nightshift Cyanide Hour blends authored RGB art. Neither inspected callable accepts camera angle or time of day; actual lighting response needs checking on the car.
articles.what: Four exact active identities were checked against the filtered picker and final runtime functions: chameleon_amethyst, chameleon_arctic, chameleon_copper and nsx_cyanide_hour. The three Chameleon functions build an RGB field, apply micro-value detail and blend it with source paint through mask and paint strength; their spec function builds M/R/Cc fields. Cyanide Hour blends authored art with supplied RGB using mask×paint strength and supplies its own spec map. These inspected functions do not take camera angle or track time as input. This does not prove the lit material looks identical across views, but it does not establish automatic camera-driven hue rotation or a day/night paint swap. Choose by the actual paint, channels, target and car appearance rather than a family name. Historical shelf counts, average channels and universal scale/day/night rules are not verified by this review.
when: You want a multi-colour material look and can compare its actual result.
You need to protect printed sponsor RGB before selecting a colour-bearing finish.
how: Select the Zone and verify its intended artwork coverage. Open the Base Material library and inspect the current Chameleon Amethyst, Chameleon Arctic or Chameleon Copper entries.
These reviewed identities can carry RGB paint as well as material data. Choose the colour source deliberately and keep sponsor/number coverage outside an intended body colour change.
Inspect the paint and the separate metallic, roughness and clearcoat views. A family name does not establish camera-driven RGB hue rotation or an automatic day/night paint swap.
Adjust the relevant detail and colour controls, then compare the actual car at the distance and lighting you intend. A generated field or catalog preview is not finished-car approval.
tips: A static multi-colour texture and changing specular illumination are different mechanisms.
pitfalls: A shift name does not guarantee two named colours at every angle.
Do not assume all shift finishes preserve RGB, need a dark base, or fail above one fixed scale.

deep.heading: COLOR FLIP changes baked RGB
deep.body: The inspected Color Lab computes YIQ hue rotation on the dark-value population of RGB paint. It takes a degree value, not a camera angle. Value weighting, gamut clipping, depth, source colour and contribution mean 180 does not guarantee an exact perceptual opposite at every pixel. The Color Lab path is selected when base_color_depth is not None.

faq.q: Does increasing Base Scale always kill every colour-shift finish?
faq.a: No universal threshold is established. Scale changes sampled texture structure, not an automatic hue-shift switch. Compare the exact finish at the intended car size and distance; strength changes contribution rather than feature size.

faq.q: Can Chameleon Amethyst change the RGB colours of my sponsors?
faq.a: Yes, its reviewed paint function builds and blends its own RGB field wherever it contributes. Protect the intended target and check the composition. Ordinary primary source-paint mode skips that paint function, but other contributors can still change artwork.

faq.q: How should I compare a shift finish without assuming it works in every light?
faq.a: Compare its actual paint and M/R/Cc images, then the composed car under relevant lighting and views. Check sponsor legibility and colour changes separately. The four inspected functions establish construction, not universal native appearance.

deep.heading: Two families of Fractured
deep.body: The Fractured series splits by their spec. The mirror-carrier shelves (Minds 55, Souls 30, Forge 88, Opalfire 50) average metal 233 to 242 and coat 237 to 252, with roughness 31 to 61: the night-carrier state that reads hot pink in a spec picture. The colour-detail shelves (Elements 60, Cosmos 60, Nightshift 50, Flames 75, Wilds 110, Tessera 50, Relics 50) average much lower metal, from 57 to 156.

deep.heading: Why a carrier is not one flat fill
deep.body: A Fractured carrier uses metal 242 to 255, roughness 22 to 78 and coat 246 to 255. A single flat magenta fill looks dead; the good ones use 6 to 8 or more quantised carriers, crushed dark shades, black pits and thin bright veins, and white clear-coat razor lips of 40, 16, 16 in 2 to 6 pixel lines. Hologram-type cells take discrete states in 8 to 18 pixel cells.

deep.heading: Mortal Shokk and Neon Underground
deep.body: Mortal Shokk has 26 finishes built on 4K plates, each with its own hand-built spec map. Neon Underground has 25 street-racing neon finishes whose fine coloured detail averages metal 60, roughness 81 and coat 123. Both are fine structural colour and both bring their own colours.

deep.heading: How advice is chosen
deep.body: Stored cards support word and synonym retrieval. The ranker adds role, goal, authored ratings, atlas quality and palette preferences, widens thin retrieval and diversifies candidates. Different advice for numbers, thin trim and full body reflects those heuristics.

deep.heading: Evidence limits
deep.body: Pair and avoid fields are metadata, not tested layer combinations. Missing rating fields fall back to3; deep notes can be absent. Optional semantic data can fail while keyword search continues. Check active exact identity rather than a historical catalog count.

faq.q: Does the advisor need an AI key?
faq.a: No. It answers free and offline from the cards.

faq.q: What does risk mean?
faq.a: How easily the finish goes wrong, such as on numbers or in the wrong colour.

faq.q: What is the difference between loud and busy?
faq.a: Loud is attention-grabbing colour or shine; busy is lots of small detail.

faq.q: Does a finish change handling?
faq.a: No.

mistakes.symptom: Several loud, busy finishes fight each other.
mistakes.cause: Too many hero finishes.
mistakes.fix: One hero, then its paired finishes.

mistakes.symptom: A pair did not work on my colour.
mistakes.cause: Pairs ignore your colour.
mistakes.fix: Preview with See on paint.

protips: Pick one hero finish, then take its paired finishes for the rest of the car.
The avoid list is as valuable as the pair list.

articles.title: What makes a finish pop
articles.summary: Compare paint-palette contrast, material response and readability separately. Combined spec RGB is channel data; choosing the colour opposite of the paint is not a verified way to make the finish pop.
articles.what: Red, green and blue in a combined spec picture encode metallic, roughness and clearcoat rather than decorative colour. Make paint-palette choices separately from material values and texture. A focal area with calmer neighbours can be a design option, but there is no universal best-looking formula. Verify target coverage, source colour protection and actual car readability before accepting a recommendation.
when: Your car looks flat
You are choosing between two finishes
how: Decide what the paint palette should communicate and which numbers or sponsors need clarity.
Compare material contrast by reading individual spec channels, not the display colour of the combined map.
Check the actual car at relevant distances and lighting before accepting the design.
tips: Fine-detail targets express the owner’s design preference, not calibrated UV geometry or per-car physical dimensions.
pitfalls: A complementary display colour in the combined spec map does not establish complementary paint colour or a suitable material.
aliases: why does my finish look boring

deep.heading: Suggestion versus evidence
deep.body: Focal areas, restrained palettes and contrasting neighbours are design options. Source channel facts do not prove that any one arrangement looks best on every car.

faq.q: Is more colour better?
faq.a: No. Two or three colours plus one accent.

faq.q: Is chrome good on a whole car?
faq.a: It is loud and shows every flaw. It suits accents.

faq.q: How do I make black pop?
faq.a: Add a flake spec pattern or a candy accent; black beside hot pink or white contrasts strongly.

faq.q: Does it look the same in the sim?
faq.a: Judge on a track in sun, shade and night, and at replay distance.

mistakes.symptom: Looks cool in the thumbnail, muddy on the car.
mistakes.cause: Mid-tone mud at thumbnail size stays mud.
mistakes.fix: Add value contrast or shine contrast between neighbours.

mistakes.symptom: Everything glossy and flat.
mistakes.cause: One material everywhere.
mistakes.fix: Give neighbours the opposite shine.

protips: A chrome pinstripe on a matte car reads as real chrome.
If a finish does not show up, add more small events and more channel contrast; do not make the marks bigger.

articles.title: Base strength, hue, saturation and brightness
articles.summary: Base Strength mixes primary paint separately from Spec Strength. Hue/Saturation/Brightness tune colour within coverage; other contributors and colour-mode choices still matter for source protection.
articles.what: BASE STRENGTH fades the whole base look over your source paint: 0 is your original paint, 100 percent is the full finish. HUE SHIFT turns every colour around the wheel from -180 to 180 degrees. SATURATION runs from -100 (greyer) to 100 (more vivid). BRIGHTNESS runs from -100 (darker) to 200 (brighter). Each has a reset arrow.
when: The colour is almost right
You want a hint of the finish instead of full coverage
how: Select the zone and open BASE.
Drag BASE STRENGTH down to let your paint through.
Use HUE SHIFT, SATURATION and BRIGHTNESS to tune the colour.

controls.label: BASE STRENGTH
controls.effect: Fades the finish over your paint.

tips: Use the separate Spec Strength for material contribution, and inspect its neutral-channel interpolation. Source mode skips the reviewed ordinary primary paint pass; Base Strength alone is not a universal whole-render paint lock.
pitfalls: Lowering BASE STRENGTH also lowers colour changes, not just shine.

deep.heading: The formulas
deep.body: Hue shift rotates every hue by the chosen degrees, from minus 180 to plus 180. Saturation becomes saturation times (1 plus the slider over 100). Brightness becomes value times (1 plus the slider over 100). Both are clipped to the legal range. If all three sliders are under half a unit, the step is skipped. The tuning only applies inside the zone mask. Measured: on a green finish, plus 180 gave magenta, minus 150 hot pink and plus 150 purple. Greys have no hue and need a colour mode.

deep.heading: BASE STRENGTH mixes paint only
deep.body: BASE STRENGTH mixes the finished base look over your original paint: output = original times (1 minus a) plus result times a, where a is the zone mask times the strength. At 0 you see your original paint; at 100 percent the full base. It never changes the shine, which is the job of SPEC STRENGTH. Patterns are added after the strength mix, so lowering BASE STRENGTH does not dim them.

deep.heading: Which control for which complaint
deep.body: More subtle: BASE STRENGTH or intensity. Less shiny: SPEC STRENGTH. Smaller pattern: scale, not strength. Too dark: brightness plus 30 to plus 40. Leaning violet: hue minus 15. Grey with a tint: saturation minus 10. Each slider has a reset arrow.

examples.title: Tame a loud finish
examples.goal: Keep part of your original paint.
examples.result: 60 percent of the finish over 40 percent of your own colours.

examples.title: Fix a navy tint
examples.goal: Get an own-colour finish to look like the swatch.
examples.result: Lighter, less purple version without losing the design.

combos.why: The mode decides what the sliders act on.
The shine counterpart of Base Strength.

faq.q: Does BASE STRENGTH change shine?
faq.a: No. Only colour.

faq.q: Why did hue shift not work on grey?
faq.a: Greys have no hue.

faq.q: Does hue shift change my numbers?
faq.a: Only inside the zone, and numbers are protected when they sit on their own layer.

faq.q: What is the range of brightness?
faq.a: Minus 100 to plus 200.

mistakes.symptom: Lowering BASE STRENGTH dulled the colours.
mistakes.cause: It lets your original paint show through.
mistakes.fix: Use hue, saturation and brightness for colour changes.

mistakes.symptom: Pattern did not fade with Base Strength.
mistakes.cause: Patterns come after the mix.
mistakes.fix: Lower the pattern opacity.

protips: Hue shift is relative to the current hue, so work in small steps.
Right control for the job: more subtle means base strength, less shiny means spec strength, smaller pattern means scale.

articles.title: Colour scale, depth, flip and underglow
articles.summary: COLOR DEPTH, COLOR FLIP and UNDERGLOW are RGB colour treatments. Touching a Lab dial initializes depth to 65% if absent and pins colour strength to 1. Depth zero does not disable active Flip or Underglow; reset depth returns to 65%, not off.
articles.what: The active UI initializes the colour lab on any Lab-dial interaction: absent depth becomes 0.65, absent flip/underglow become zero, and colour strength becomes 1. Serializer includes the Lab values only when depth is present; the inspected compositor uses that presence to choose the Lab path. Depth controls a value-driven RGB tint calculation, not actual physical coat thickness. At depth zero the candy blend weight is zero, but Flip and Underglow have separate branches and can still alter RGB. Reset Depth sets 0.65; Reset Flip sets only flip to zero while retaining Lab activation and depth. Flip applies dark-value-weighted YIQ rotation; 90/180 are degree settings, not guaranteed neighbouring/opposite perceived hues at every pixel. Underglow screen-blends a gold/silver-like RGB field based on the mean chosen colour and underlying brightness; it does not create a light object or under-car illumination. Other composition contributors still matter for exact paint colour. Historical gradient-shelf counts are not verified by this control review.
when: You want a candy look
You want a two-tone flip
how: Before changing exact brand colours, inspect whether depth is absent or the colour lab is already active.
Use depth for colour treatment, Flip for dark-value hue treatment and Underglow for the ground-colour RGB blend.
Check all three values when reversing a Lab change; zeroing or resetting one is not a complete off switch.
Use Undo to return to the state before Lab interaction when appropriate, then verify the composed RGB and other contributors.

controls.label: COLOR DEPTH
controls.default: off (handle rests at 65%; first touch turns it on at 65%)
controls.effect: Controls the candy RGB blend. Zero removes this blend, but Flip and Underglow may still act.

controls.label: COLOR FLIP
controls.effect: Degree setting for dark-value-weighted YIQ hue rotation; not live camera-angle input.

controls.label: UNDERGLOW
controls.effect: Gold/silver-like RGB screen blend; no emitted light.

controls.label: COLOR SCALE and ROTATION
controls.range: scale and rotation of the colour art

tips: A plain colour pick does not itself activate the Lab, but it also does not clear existing Lab fields. Inspect Depth/Flip/Underglow and later contributors before claiming exact RGB.
pitfalls: A reset on a Lab dial keeps its activation/default fields; it is not a complete Source-paint switch.
Choosing Solid Color again does not clear an already active Lab treatment.
The gradient CSS bar does not preview full material, coverage, overlays or lighting.
aliases: how can i build a gradient

deep.heading: Activation versus zero
deep.body: A missing depth and an explicit depth of zero are different payload states. The UI ensures depth before setting or resetting another Lab dial. At depth zero, candy alpha is zero; independent Flip and Underglow branches still run if their values are positive. Thus zero depth alone does not restore the pre-Lab exact-colour path.

deep.heading: Reset semantics
deep.body: Reset Depth writes 0.65 after ensuring the Lab exists. Reset Flip writes zero only to Flip, while Ensure may initialize depth to0.65 and strength1. These are parameter resets, not an off switch for the whole pipeline.

deep.heading: No physical light or coat guarantee
deep.body: The inspected helper calculates RGB arrays from paint value and chosen colour. It creates no physical coating geometry or scene light. Test the actual paint and material response rather than treating the controls as measured coat thickness, exact perceived hue travel or night illumination.

faq.q: Why are the sliders greyed out?
faq.a: BASE COLOR must be solid, gradient or from special.

faq.q: Does COLOR FLIP 180 guarantee an exact opposite hue on every paint pixel?
faq.a: No. The inspected Color Lab rotates RGB through YIQ and weights the result toward the underlying dark-value population. Gamut clipping, value weighting, source colour, depth and contribution affect the output. It is a baked colour treatment, not camera-driven hue rotation or a universal perceptual opposite.

faq.q: Does roughness flip the red and white paint colours?
faq.a: Roughness is encoded in the green spec channel. It changes material response rather than exchanging red and white decorative paint RGB. Reflected appearance can change without RGB repainting. COLOR FLIP is a separate colour treatment; a roughness value is not a paint-colour swap command.

faq.q: Does setting COLOR DEPTH to zero disable COLOR FLIP and UNDERGLOW too?
faq.a: No. Zero depth removes the candy blend, but the inspected Flip and Underglow branches can still alter RGB when their values are positive. Depth zero also remains an active Lab payload state; it is not the same as absent depth.

faq.q: Does Reset COLOR DEPTH turn the colour lab off?
faq.a: No. The active reset handler sets depth to65% after ensuring the Lab is initialized. It does not remove the depth field or turn off the Lab pipeline.

faq.q: Why did touching COLOR FLIP darken my exact brand colour?
faq.a: The active UI initializes missing depth to65% and pins colour strength to1 when a Lab dial is touched. This activates a value-driven colour treatment in addition to Flip. Check Depth, Flip, Underglow and the composed paint; changing a single dial is not an exact-colour preservation guarantee.

faq.q: Does UNDERGLOW create actual lights beneath my car?
faq.a: No. In the inspected Color Lab, Underglow is a gold/silver-like screen blend inside RGB paint. It creates no scene light or under-car illumination. Actual visibility under track lighting still needs checking.

faq.q: If I reset COLOR FLIP to zero, is my original exact RGB colour restored?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Reset Flip clears only its degree value and ensures Lab initialization; Depth and Underglow can remain active, along with other contributors. To recover a prior exact-colour state, compare with the state before Lab interaction and verify the final RGB.

mistakes.symptom: Depth is zero but the paint still looks treated.
mistakes.cause: Flip, Underglow or other contributors may remain active.
mistakes.fix: Inspect all Lab values and other contributors; compare with the pre-change state.

protips: Check exact source RGB and the final composed paint before accepting a brand-colour match.

articles.title: Base scale and rotation
articles.summary: BASE SCALE changes generated finish placement/detail, including coloured texture when the paint path generates it. Ordinary primary Source paint skips that paint pass and its placement; Spec Scale follows Base Scale unless independent. It does not resize the car or imported PSD layer. In the explicit primary colour path, Base Scale multiplies Colour Scale.
articles.what: Primary BASE SCALE and SPEC SCALE are linked by default. The active link normalizes them from 0.05 to 5.00 in 0.05 steps. Below 1.00, generated material detail is tiled more finely; this is not resizing the car or a PSD layer. Independent spec scale changes spec placement while leaving the paint-scale setting alone. Colour Scale has a separate paint path: the explicit base-colour path uses BASE SCALE multiplied by Colour Scale. Do not assume two sliders at 0.50 produce an effective 0.50 there. A source-passing base must not tile the source car artwork just because BASE SCALE is reduced.
when: Carbon, flake or camo looks too large
The texture runs the wrong way
how: Confirm the selected zone and the finish actually generating the detail you want to resize.
For finer generated base detail, reduce BASE SCALE in small steps and inspect the result.
To resize material detail while keeping paint placement, enable INDEPENDENT SPEC and adjust SPEC SCALE instead.
For a second through fifth base, distinguish Colour Scale, Spec Scale and its scatter/distribution Scale; choose the one matching the detail.
tips: Fine detail is an owner preference, not a universal scale preset. A ratio such as 0.50 repeats a generated tile more often; it does not guarantee a particular pixel feature size on every finish.
Keep sponsor artwork on its source paint path when changing material appearance. A different spec can change how that colour looks under light even when the paint pixels are preserved.
pitfalls: Do not lower Spec Strength to make a texture smaller: it changes material values, not the geometric scale.
A constant plain Foundation material has no internal grain to resize. Plain Foundation Brushed and Metallic do not generate the decorative grain or glitter their names might suggest.
Do not apply a PSD layer resize to solve a finish-texture question. That resizes artwork.

deep.body: Primary BASE SCALE and SPEC SCALE are linked by default. The active link normalizes them from 0.05 to 5.00 in 0.05 steps. Below 1.00, generated material detail is tiled more finely; this is not resizing the car or a PSD layer. Independent spec scale changes spec placement while leaving the paint-scale setting alone. Colour Scale has a separate paint path: the explicit base-colour path uses BASE SCALE multiplied by Colour Scale. Do not assume two sliders at 0.50 produce an effective 0.50 there. A source-passing base must not tile the source car artwork just because BASE SCALE is reduced.

faq.q: If base scale and colour scale are both 0.50, is colour scale effectively 0.25?
faq.a: Yes, in the explicit base-colour path those factors multiply: 0.50 × 0.50 = 0.25 effective colour scale. This is scoped to that path, not a universal claim about every material or overlay.

faq.q: Does changing base scale resize my whole car?
faq.a: No. BASE SCALE changes generated finish placement/detail; it is not the PSD layer resize control. For a source-passing finish, reducing it must not tile your imported car artwork.

faq.q: How do I keep my paint and resize only its material texture?
faq.a: Enable INDEPENDENT SPEC for the selected zone, then adjust SPEC SCALE. This separates spec placement from paint placement; check that the finish has spec detail to resize.

faq.q: Are Base Scale and Colour Scale the same slider?
faq.a: No. In the explicit base-colour path their factors multiply: BASE SCALE 0.50 and Colour Scale 0.50 give effective colour scale 0.25. Keep the other control in mind when diagnosing size.

faq.q: Does half scale mean exactly half-size features everywhere?
faq.a: It is a placement/repetition factor, not a measured feature-size guarantee across every finish or UV layout. Inspect the chosen finish and the actual car; finer repeats do not identify mapped car parts.

faq.q: Which overlay size control changes texture rather than dust distribution?
faq.a: Use the additional base’s Spec Scale for material texture, or Colour Scale for its paint texture. Its scatter/distribution Scale controls the noise-mode coverage field; it is not a universal material-texture resize.

faq.q: Can Base Scale resize my imported sponsors in Source paint mode?
faq.a: The reviewed ordinary primary Source paint path skips both its base-paint generation and base-paint placement. Changing Base Scale there should not tile or resize imported sponsor artwork. Linked spec detail may still change; extra bases, patterns, colour adjustments and PSD transforms are separate contributors.

faq.q: Does Base Scale never affect coloured detail?
faq.a: That is too broad. It can change the placement/repetition of generated coloured finish detail. In the explicit primary colour path, Base Scale multiplies Colour Scale; Source paint skips the ordinary primary base-paint pass instead. This is not a car or PSD-layer resize.

mistakes: Do not lower Spec Strength to make a texture smaller: it changes material values, not the geometric scale.
A constant plain Foundation material has no internal grain to resize. Plain Foundation Brushed and Metallic do not generate the decorative grain or glitter their names might suggest.
Do not apply a PSD layer resize to solve a finish-texture question. That resizes artwork.
protips: Fine detail is an owner preference, not a universal scale preset. A ratio such as 0.50 repeats a generated tile more often; it does not guarantee a particular pixel feature size on every finish.
Keep sponsor artwork on its source paint path when changing material appearance. A different spec can change how that colour looks under light even when the paint pixels are preserved.

articles.title: Second base and overlays
articles.summary: Second through fifth bases can mix paint and material over the primary. A fresh second base starts at 100 percent strength, so inspect colour source before preserving artwork. Without a pattern mask, pattern-driven blending falls back to a uniform mix; colour/spec texture scales differ from dust scatter scale.
articles.what: A zone can hold one primary base plus second through fifth base overlays. An overlay can contribute paint and material; its colour source, colour strength, material strength and blend mode are separate choices. Pattern-driven blend modes use a pattern mask when available; without one, the current alpha calculation falls back to a uniform blend rather than making the overlay invisible. A fresh second base starts at 100 percent strength and chooses Pattern-Pop when the zone has a pattern, otherwise Tint. This can immediately cover the previous paint, so lower its strength and inspect the colour source when preserving artwork. Distinguish Fractal Dust scatter scale from the overlay colour texture scale and its independently selectable spec scale. Current additional-base spec preparation is gated by its Spec Strength, not its Paint Strength. A valid registered additional base with paint strength0 and spec strength100 can remain active for material. The current second-through-fifth spec mixer uses a per-pixel normalized weight budget; paint overlays are a separate process.
when: Chrome flake over candy
Matte clear on gloss
how: Select the intended zone and open OVERLAYS.
Pick an additional base and inspect its colour source.
Lower strength and compare before committing to a strong paint or material mix.
Choose the blend mode, then adjust colour texture scale or independent spec scale for the appropriate target.
tips: Start with Tint (subtle) at a low strength.
pitfalls: Every overlay adds render time and visual noise.

An overlay can contribute paint and material; its colour source, colour strength, material strength and blend mode are separate choices. Pattern-driven blend modes use a pattern mask when available; without one, the current alpha calculation falls back to a uniform blend rather than making the overlay invisible. A fresh second base starts at 100 percent strength and chooses Pattern-Pop when the zone has a pattern, otherwise Tint. This can immediately cover the previous paint, so lower its strength and inspect the colour source when preserving artwork. Current additional-base spec preparation is gated by its Spec Strength, not its Paint Strength. A valid registered additional base with paint strength0 and spec strength100 can remain active for material. examples.title: Pearl on gloss
examples.goal: Depth without losing the base.
examples.result: A soft pearl shimmer on the gloss body.

examples.title: Edge glow
examples.goal: Make the pattern edges light up.
examples.result: The overlay shows along the pattern edges.

Pattern-driven modes need a pattern.

faq.q: Can I keep a second base spec with its paint strength at zero?
faq.a: Yes for a valid registered additional base in the current weighted paths. Paint Strength 0 stops its paint contribution, while positive Spec Strength can keep its material contribution. Primary Use source paint does not replace the additional-base paint strength control.

faq.q: How many bases can a zone have?
faq.a: Up to five in all: one base plus four overlays.

faq.q: Why does my pattern-driven mode do nothing?
faq.a: If there is no pattern mask, the current pattern-driven alpha falls back to a uniform blend. If the overlay is invisible, inspect its strength, selected base and colour source, zone coverage, material contribution and whether the target differs from what is underneath. An available pattern shapes where the blend occurs.

faq.q: Does overlay scale matter?
faq.a: Identify the scale first. Fractal Dust/noise scatter scale changes the blend mask. Overlay colour scale changes its paint texture, and independent spec scale can change its material texture separately. Scaling a plain constant material does not create grain.

faq.q: Which mode to start with?
faq.a: Tint (subtle) at a low strength.

faq.q: How do I stack a second base over the first?
faq.a: Open OVERLAYS and choose a second base. Check its colour source and lower its strength before judging how it mixes with existing artwork. Choose a blend mode; the current fresh-add default is Pattern-Pop with a pattern or Tint without one. A zone has primary plus four additional base tiers, each distinct from its spec-overlay stack.

faq.q: Why does Pattern-Pop show a solid wash when I have no pattern?
faq.a: The current engine uses a uniform alpha when no pattern mask is available, even for pattern-driven modes. At 50 percent overlay strength it is a half blend within a fully covered zone. Add a suitable pattern if you want the mode to react to pattern structure; first inspect the colour source and strength.

faq.q: Why did adding a second base cover my original paint?
faq.a: A fresh second base starts at 100 percent strength, with its own colour source and a blend default of Pattern-Pop when a pattern exists or Tint otherwise. Without a pattern, uniform blending can fully cover the previous paint. Lower strength and select the intended colour source; do not assume a second base changes shine only.

faq.q: Is a second base the same as a spec overlay?
faq.a: No. A second base can contribute paint and material. A spec overlay adds material texture to selected channels and does not repaint pixels. Each base tier can have its own separate spec-overlay stack.

faq.q: Does second base strength zero leave its spec contribution on?
faq.a: If you mean Paint Strength, yes: zero paint strength can still leave a valid additional base’s spec active when Spec Strength is positive. The current weighted spec path is gated by Spec Strength, not Paint Strength. Set its Spec Strength to zero to remove that material contribution; inspect other contributors separately.

faq.q: Why does changing overlay scatter scale not resize its paint texture?
faq.a: Scatter scale controls the blend-mask distribution for noise/dust blending. Overlay colour scale controls the paint texture itself; independent spec scale controls material texture. Use the scale for the target you want to resize.

faq.q: Can I scale second base material detail without resizing its paint?
faq.a: The overlay has a separate spec-scale choice: independent spec scale separates it from colour scale. A plain material with constant channels has no grain or flake to resize. Compare a textured material in the spec views.

faq.q: Does choosing Tint mean my original colours are protected?
faq.a: No. Tint describes blend coverage, not guaranteed source-colour protection. Without a pattern it is a uniform blend whose strength can reach full replacement. Check the overlay colour source, lower strength and protect sponsor material separately.

faq.q: Will a pattern blend affect pixels outside my zone?
faq.a: The alpha calculation multiplies by the provided zone mask: zero mask coverage leaves zero blend alpha and soft coverage reduces it. This is a blend-stage property, not a guarantee that unrelated later operations cannot change the same pixels.

faq.q: Can Pattern-Pop work without a pattern?
faq.a: It can contribute a uniform blend without a pattern mask. The available pattern mask shapes the effect when present. The current fresh second-base default is Pattern-Pop when a pattern exists, otherwise Tint; both can change paint depending on colour source and strength.

faq.q: Does a second base only change shine?
faq.a: No. A second base can contribute paint and spec. Check the overlay colour source and strength before adding it over artwork. Material-only spec overlays are a separate feature.

mistakes.symptom: The overlay washed out the base.
mistakes.cause: Strength too high.
mistakes.fix: Lower strength to 30 to 40.

mistakes.symptom: Render got slow.
mistakes.cause: Every overlay adds work.
mistakes.fix: Remove unused overlays.

protips: Old saved looks that used removed modes are mapped to a kept mode, so they still render.
Overlay alpha is linear in strength, which makes it predictable: half strength is half the overlay.

articles.title: Wear: scuffed and aged looks
articles.summary: Wear is a stored per-zone value from 0 to 100 that the engine turns into chips, scratches and a duller clearcoat. This build has no Wear slider and Season mode is retired, so you get a worn look from a worn Base Material and Base Strength.
articles.what: Wear is a number from 0 to 100 kept on each zone. When a zone has wear above 0, the render engine adds chips, scratches and a duller clearcoat to that zone. In this build nothing in the Pro window sets it: the zone card has no Wear slider, and the old Season set-up (add races, Quick: Wear Ramp, Render All Races) is retired. Its panel stays hidden and nothing opens it. To get a worn look today, pick a worn finish as the zone's Base Material, lower Base Strength so your own paint shows through, and add chip or scuff spec overlays.
when: A race-worn, barn-find or sun-faded look
You wonder where the Wear slider and Season mode went
how: Make or pick the zone to age: Remaining on Car Paint, or APPLY AREA > Draw box on the lower body, front or roof.
Under BASE press Base Material and search a worn finish: Sun Faded, Die-Back Patina, Hardware: Battle Worn or Surface Rust.
Lower Base Strength to 50 to 70 so your own colours show through (0 is your paint, 100 is the full finish).
For chips and scuffs open BASE > SPEC OVERLAYS and add Micro Chipping or Scuffed Enamel at Strength 30 to 40.
Press RENDER and check at 100 percent zoom: wear should read as fine detail, not blotches.

controls.label: Base Strength
controls.effect: How much of the worn finish replaces your own paint.

tips: Sun Faded and Surface Rust are on the Foundation EFX shelf, Die-Back Patina on SHOKK WORKS and Hardware: Battle Worn on TACTICAL & FIELD, so searching by name is quickest.
Desert Worn, Barn Find and Rally Mud exist in the catalogue but are not listed in the Base Material picker. Ask the Shokker AI helper for them by name.
pitfalls: High Base Strength with a heavy worn finish hides your own colours and fine detail.

deep.heading: What wear does, by level
deep.body: These are the engine's values, whoever sets them. Wear runs 0 to 100. 0 is showroom fresh. About 25 is light track wear with micro-scratches. 50 is mid-season with visible scratches, rougher surfaces and chips. 75 is heavy use. 100 is a track-beaten veteran. Scratches are horizontal-biased: roughness goes up by as much as 60 times the wear fraction and metal goes down by as much as 30 times it. Wear also DULLS the clearcoat (the coat byte goes up toward 255, never toward the glossy end): on average a matte base goes from 153 at wear 0 to 176 at 50 and 198 at 100, a satin from 67 to 90 to 114, and a gloss from 16 to 39 to 63. Edges wear a little more. Above 20 percent, chips desaturate and slightly brighten damaged areas. Above 30 percent, edges where colours meet wear more, with extra roughness and metal loss.

deep.heading: How it is applied
deep.body: The wear step runs once at the highest wear level among your zones and is blended per zone by that zone's level over the maximum, only where the zone owns the pixel. After wear the iron rules are applied again, so the result is always legal. The render engine also has an all-in-one export that takes one global wear level (helmet 20 lower, suit 40 lower), but the booth window has no control for it.

deep.heading: Where the controls went
deep.body: A zone still stores a wear value, and the render path sends it to the engine whenever it is above 0. Zone setups save it. But the Pro window no longer has anything that sets it: the zone card shows Base Strength and no Wear slider. The Season panel (Add Race, Quick: Wear Ramp, Render All Races) is hidden and nothing opens it, and Render All Races only shows a message that Season mode is disabled in this booth build. The MCP zone-edit tool has Base Strength and Spec Strength but no wear option, and the Shokker AI helper has no wear setting in its edit code either.

deep.heading: The look you can get today
deep.body: Pick the worn finish by the story you want. Sun Faded is broad bleached zones over a fine dust-pitted skin, an unevenly sun-bleached panel. Die-Back Patina is a dusty aged earth-tone surface of collapsed matte patches with faint glossy lips. Hardware: Battle Worn is a dark olive-brown surface with heavy speckled wear and pale chips. Surface Rust is rust blooming through the paint in spots. Lower Base Strength to keep your own colours, then add Micro Chipping or Scuffed Enamel from BASE > SPEC OVERLAYS for chips and scuffs.

deep.heading: Wear needs detail to hide
deep.body: Fine finishes lose their detail under heavy wear, because chips and scratches cover it. Worn finishes already carry the damage, so a strong worn base needs few overlays.

faq.q: Why is there no Wear slider?

faq.q: What happened to Season mode, Add Race and Quick: Wear Ramp?

articles.summary: For the exact plain Foundation identities, Gloss starts M/R/CC0/30/16, Satin0/95/70, Matte0/200/160, Pearl100/40/16, Metallic200/50/16, Candy200/15/16 and Chrome255/2/16. These are encoded material values, not physical metal percentages, paint transparency or guaranteed simulator appearances.
articles.what: The reviewed exact plain Foundation registrations bind a constant three-channel spec function and paint_none. Pearl and Metallic differ in encoded metallic value; Candy and Metallic share M200 but start at R15 and R50 respectively. Gloss has lower starting roughness than Satin. Lower roughness generally sharpens reflections, but paint colour, clearcoat, strength, later contributors, the specific car and lighting affect the final appearance. The title Candy does not make paint alpha transparent or change car geometry, and Chrome does not prove a perfect mirror on every car. Some differently identified, similarly named finishes have spatially varying spec; their registry values are not proof of every output pixel or verified means. Foundation also includes reviewed colour-bearing gem/shift entries, so the entire shelf is not universally paint-none.

pitfalls: M100 is an encoded metallic value, not proof of half-metal physical composition.

faq.q: What is the difference between metallic and pearl?
faq.a: For exact plain Foundation f_metallic and f_pearl, starting M/R/CC is200/50/16 versus100/40/16. Those are encoded material settings, not physical metal fractions. Both use constant material maps here, not visible flake geometry.

faq.q: Candy or metallic, what is the difference?
faq.a: Exact plain Foundation f_candy and f_metallic both start M200 and CC16; Candy starts R15, Metallic R50. This changes the material baseline, not paint alpha or car geometry. Inspect the actual lit result.

faq.q: Does Foundation Pearl metal100 mean the car is physically half metal?
faq.a: No.100 is an encoded metallic-channel value on a0–255 scale, not a measured physical percentage or composition. The reviewed plain Foundation Pearl starts100/40/16.

faq.q: Does Foundation Candy make my body transparent like glass?
faq.a: No transparency is established by this material. Exact plain Foundation Candy starts M/R/CC200/15/16 and uses paint_none; it does not set paint alpha or modify car geometry. Its name describes a material look, not a glass-body guarantee.

faq.q: Is Foundation Chrome guaranteed to be a perfect mirror on every car?
faq.a: No. Its reviewed plain starting spec is255/2/16. Final reflections depend on the actual car, paint and lighting, strength and later contributors; a universal perfect mirror is not verified.

faq.q: If I pick a metallic name outside Foundation, can I assume its spec is200/50/16 everywhere?
faq.a: No. Use the exact identity and source contract. A textured finish may generate spatially varying spec; a registry anchor or similarly named card does not prove constant pixels or current measured means.

faq.q: Does plain Foundation Metallic already include visible metal flakes?
faq.a: No. Exact f_metallic is pinned to a constant plain spec map and paint_none. Visible flake geometry needs a separately verified textured construction; no specific alternative is accepted as a native recommendation here.

faq.q: Which has lower starting roughness, Foundation Gloss or Satin?
faq.a: Gloss starts R30, Satin R95. Their full M/R/CC is0/30/16 and0/95/70. This compares starting encoded material values; the final car appearance still depends on other contributors and lighting.

articles.summary: Second through fifth bases have independent paint and spec contributions. Zero paint strength can leave spec active; material weights mix per pixel and normalize above a full budget.
articles.what: For valid additional bases in the current ordinary single and stacked weighted paths, Spec Strength controls whether the material is prepared; Paint Strength does not gate that preparation. If they exceed 1, overlays normalize proportionally and the primary has zero remaining weight there. Final channel safety clamps and uint8 conversion still apply. faq.q: Can I find a finish by its ID or tags rather than its displayed name?
faq.a: The active filter combines card name, search metadata, description, finish ID and tags into its search haystack. An ID or tag can therefore locate a card when those attributes are populated. This is card metadata search, not recognition of actual rendered pixels.

faq.q: Why do two search words give fewer results than either word alone?
faq.a: A multi-term search requires all normalized query tokens to match the card’s combined metadata. Token order does not matter. Start with one distinctive word, then add another to narrow the result; two words are not an either-word search.

faq.q: Why does a one-word search show related words I did not type?
faq.a: A single query token can expand to a configured synonym family and match any member. Multi-word queries keep the all-token rule instead. This broadening is metadata matching, not a recommendation that each result is suitable for your car.

faq.q: Why does searching for a known finish still give no result in Favorites?
faq.a: Text matching, the active filter and any category context must all pass. Searching does not bypass Favorites. Choose All and clear guided category context when checking whether a known card exists in the current picker.

faq.q: Why did clicking All not remove my search words?
faq.a: Changing the filter to All clears the active lane context, but reuses the current search input. Clear the search text separately if you want the full current card set. All refers to the filter, not an automatic search reset.

faq.q: Why is the ranked count larger than the number of shown results?
faq.a: Shown counts cards that pass the active search/filter/context. Ranked counts positive-ranked cards encountered across the grid, including cards hidden by that search. The two numbers describe different populations; ranked is not a count of visible approved recommendations.

faq.q: Why did several category groups open when I searched?
faq.a: A nonempty query or a filter other than All removes the collapsed class from result groups. Groups with no matching cards are hidden. This lets you inspect the matching cards; it does not change a finish or apply material to your paint.

faq.q: Why does clearing search leave the category of my current finish open?
faq.a: With no query and All selected, the group containing a selected finish is opened while other populated groups are collapsed by the filter pass. The selected card determines this opening behavior; it is not a recommendation to switch categories.

faq.q: Where did the Strong, Sponsor Safe and Fast picker filter buttons go?
faq.a: The current filter-control builder exposes All, Favorites and Showcase; its sort buttons are Grouped, My Rating and A-Z. Older branches still recognize other filter names internally, but that is not proof those buttons are displayed in this popup.

faq.q: Does Showcase certify that a finish will protect my sponsor artwork?
faq.a: For ordinary cards Showcase matches an owner-status keyword or configured rank/spec/fit/confidence thresholds. The special spec-overlay branch uses an approved metadata flag and rank threshold. This filter does not inspect your document, sponsor footprint or rendered result. Verify targeting and actual output separately.

faq.q: Why did choosing a Special reset my Base paint strength, spec strength and spec blend?

faq.q: Does replacing a Special also clear my drawn selection and pattern stack?
faq.a: The reviewed monolithic helper changes material and listed strength/colour fields but does not clear regionMask, sourceLayer restrictions or patternStack. Existing primary pattern is retained, with none supplied only if it was absent. Keeping these fields does not itself prove that the composed output remains visually identical.

faq.q: Why did swapping an ordinary Base keep strength settings that a Special had reset?
faq.a: The ordinary Base helper replaces base and clears finish without the monolithic helper’s full strength reset. The outer setZoneBase still has a separate near-zero spec-strength guard. Ordinary and true-monolithic paths therefore do not have identical retention behavior.

faq.q: Will a stale out-of-range picker Zone index edit a different valid Zone?
faq.a: setZoneBase refuses a nonnumeric, negative or out-of-range index before its Undo entry and mutation. It does not redirect that invalid index to another Zone. A still-valid index pointing to a reordered Zone is a different case and is not protected by this numeric bounds check.

faq.q: Can a failed Color Lock storage write leave its flag changed without updating the button?
faq.a: toggleColorLock flips the in-memory flag first, then calls localStorage.setItem without a catch in this function.
